h: פָּרָשַׁת זָכוֹר, מַאֲמָר ג׳ Parshas Zachor — Maamar Gimmel

p: and regarding Shabbos it is written 'Remember';
so will it happen to me too.'
To what may the matter be compared? etc.
לָזֶה הִזְכַּרְתִּי עַל קְעָרָה מָלֵא כָּל טוּב
This one I mentioned over a dish full of every good thing,
and that one I mentioned over an empty dish.
So too, regarding Shabbos it is written 'Remember' etc.,
and to honor it with food, etc.;
and regarding Amalek it is written 'Remember' etc.
Over what do you remember him?
it is plausible that he used for both
for they asked him, "You mentioned this one
but here, is it not explicit—
and regarding Amalek, "You shall blot out the remembrance of Amalek"?
So how could he say that the two are equal?
is to uproot and to tear out
the root of evil and the yetzer hara,
and the mitzvah applies every year;
and nevertheless we see that it has not helped,
even with talmidei chachamim and even with the great,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר וְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
as we find with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Akiva
and it seems that it has not helped, chas v'shalom.
And a person might say: What will it help
מַה שֶּׁנִּצְטַוֵּינוּ זָכוֹר אֶת יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת לְקַדְּשׁוֹ
that we were commanded, "Remember the Shabbos day to sanctify it,"
to bring in holiness through the delight
and the holiness of the Shabbos meal—
פֶּן זֶה גַּם כֵּן לֹא יוֹעִיל
perhaps this too will not help;
"As it happens to the fool, so will it happen to me too."
And to this he answered, from the aforementioned parable,
over a dish full of every good thing;
for in truth the holiness of Shabbos
is fixed and established by Hashem Yisbarach,
"To know that I am Hashem Who sanctifies you";
for it is the day on which "Hashem gives you rest
from your sorrow and your trouble,"
that is, rest from all the enemies and the kelipos;
אַךְ אַחַר כָּךְ חוֹזֵר יֵצֶר הָרָע לִמְקוֹמוֹ
but afterward the yetzer hara returns to its place,
And one who keeps Shabbos according to its laws
is truly redeemed at once, forever.
And the mitzvah of remembrance comes
to bring in the holiness through delight,
for even the body on Shabbos is in holiness;
וְזֶהוּ עַל קְעָרָה מְלֵאָה כָּל טוּב.
and this is "over a dish full of every good thing."
Not so the remembrance of Amalek,
which is to remove the evil from the heart of the fool,
and this is mainly through avodah
and this is "over an empty table."
more of the blotting out of Amalek is accomplished,
until we merit to bring about
and to attain the blotting out of Amalek
אֲבָל כָּל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא נִמְחָה זִכְרוֹ מִכֹּל וָכֹל
But as long as his remembrance has not been completely blotted out,
However, the mitzvah of keeping Shabbos
for Hashem Yisbarach brings into Yisrael
a holiness that is fixed and established,
וְהַיִּשְׂרָאֵל מְקַדֵּשׁ הַשַּׁבָּת עַל יְדֵי הָעֹנֶג
and the Jew sanctifies Shabbos through delight,
for even the body's pleasure is in holiness.
one is saved from sin as well,
from the verse "who keeps Shabbos from profaning it
and in Pri Etz Chaim (beginning of Shaar HaShabbos),
that one is saved from the accusation of the yetzer hara
all the days of the week.
Only, a person on his part must take care
שֶׁלֹּא יִכְנוֹס הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע חַס וְשָׁלוֹם
that the yetzer hara not enter, chas v'shalom,
to spoil him in his keeping of Shabbos;
וּמִי שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לִהְיוֹת מְשַׁמֵּר שַׁבָּת כְּהִילְכָתָהּ
and one who merits to keep Shabbos according to its laws
הוּא בִּפְרָט נַפְשׁוֹ נִגְאָל מִכֹּל וָכֹל
is, as regards his own soul, completely redeemed
And on this he said (Koheles ibid. 16),
"For there is no remembrance of the wise" etc.,
is over a dish full of holiness.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Seitzei 7 — “Here it says Remember, and of Shabbos it says Remember: are the two equal? Shlomo said, 'The fate of the fool will befall me too,' and then, 'The wise person has no remembrance together with the fool forever.' ... A king made a feast and invited guests. A bowl full of every good thing was brought before him; he said, 'Remember my friend so-and-so.' After he had emptied the bowl, he said, 'Remember my enemy so-and-so.' His friends asked: 'You mentioned this one and that one!' He answered: 'I mentioned this one over a bowl full of every good thing, and that one over an empty bowl.' So of Shabbos it says, 'Remember the Shabbos day to sanctify it,' honoring it with food, drink and clean clothing. Of Amalek it says Remember; over what do you remember him? Over an empty table, as it says, 'Blot out Amalek's remembrance from beneath the heavens.'” Rav Tzadok accepts the Midrash's distinction but asks why the shared word Remember creates a difficulty when the Torah already states different purposes. He explains the full bowl as holiness granted from above and the empty bowl as the person's work of removing evil.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Beitzah 17a — “A reciter taught before Ravina: 'Who sanctifies Israel, Shabbos and the appointed times.' He said to him: 'Does Israel sanctify Shabbos? Shabbos is already sanctified and established. Rather, say: Who sanctifies Shabbos, Israel and the appointed times.' Rav Yosef said: The halachah follows Rebbi, with Ravina's correction.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: The order of the blessing preserves the distinction Rav Tzadok needs: Shabbos's holiness is already established, while Israel participates in sanctifying the festivals. This gives precise talmudic content to the full bowl's preexisting gift of holiness.

paragraphs.text: Exodus 31:13 — “You shall speak to the children of Israel, saying: You must keep My Shabbosos, for it is a sign between Me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I am Hashem who sanctifies you.” The verse expressly attributes Israel's sanctification to Hashem. Rav Tzadok distinguishes this divinely given holiness from the person's labor of removing evil.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Mei HaShiloach I, Ki Seitzei, s.v. Zachor es asher asah — “Zachor: that he remember each time how we were in bondage and how our yetzer overpowered us, and from this new desire will come to us each time.” The Izhbitzer reads the same midrash of the “empty plate” as the memory of the struggle against Amalek’s power. He adds that this very memory renews a person’s desire for Hashem’s service, which supports Rav Tzadok’s point that Amalek is erased through a person’s own avodah.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefas Emes, Pesach 5635, s.v. Va'afilu kulanu chachamim — “The final redemption will also come when all that is concealed within the Exodus has been clarified, for that redemption contains all the redemptions. ‘To bring the days of Mashiach’: remembering and recounting the Exodus brings those days. At the Exodus the intention was a complete repair, as in the future, when Hashem and His name will be one. But wicked Amalek confused Israel, as it says, ‘who encountered you on the way.’ … Through recounting the Exodus every year the repair is awakened, and his name is erased little by little.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: This gives a precise model for Rav Tzadok’s answer to the apparent failure of repeated erasure: an annual act can advance a cumulative repair whose completion is still future. Sefas Emes applies the principle to the Seder’s narration; Rav Tzadok applies it here to the yearly remembrance of Amalek.

paragraphs.text: Mechilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Beshalach, Vayassa 6 (on Shemos 16:28) — “Lest you say: Whoever keeps Shabbos, what reward does he receive? Scripture teaches: ‘Fortunate is the man who does this... who keeps Shabbos from profaning it and guards his hand from doing any evil.’ We have thus learned that whoever keeps Shabbos is kept distant from transgression.” The Yalkut Shimoni (Beshalach 261) quotes the Mechilta in Rav Tzadok's wording, מרוחק מן העבירה. The critical text reads “whoever keeps Shabbos under duress is saved from transgression” (מִדֹּחַק נֻצַּל). The passage opens parashah 6 of Vayassa. Rav Tzadok uses the teaching to affirm Shabbos's protective effect while retaining the person's duty of vigilance.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar HaShabbos 1 — “A person must intend that some of this addition remain with him for the weekdays… and he is assured that he will not sin… and the yetzer hara will not prosecute him.” The Arizal’s words give the mechanism: the added soul-light of Shabbos stays into the first three weekdays, and the coming Shabbos is drawn upon from the fourth. This is how Shabbos guards a person all week, as Rav Tzadok says here.
